metadata.title: Schooling Matters: Opportunity to Learn in PISA 2012

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper uses PISA 2012 microdata to relate student-reported Opportunity to Learn (OTL) indices to PISA mathematics literacy outcomes at multiple levels (country, school, and student). The paper discusses PISA’s sampling approach (random sampling of 15-year-olds within sampled schools) and uses hierarchical modeling to separate variation across countries, schools, and students. However, the excerpt provided does not report the specific PISA weight variables (e.g., student sampling weights) or whether replicate weights were used, so the exact weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the text. For analysts working with the PISA international database, the recommended practice is to apply the provided complex-survey student weights and replicate weights when estimating standard errors, and to use the PISA scaling/score construction documentation for the mathematics literacy outcomes.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper reports that country-level mathematics literacy means were defined using the first plausible value, but it does not document how missing data were handled in the hierarchical regressions (e.g., whether cases with missing OTL or background variables were excluded, or whether any imputation was used). This is a reporting gap because PISA datasets typically contain missingness in questionnaire responses and background variables, which can affect estimated relationships if not handled transparently. Without the missing-data strategy, the robustness of the reported OTL–performance associations to missingness assumptions cannot be fully evaluated.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The paper uses PISA 2012 mathematics literacy data and student questionnaire OTL items (formal mathematics, word problems, applied mathematics). It reports analyses at the country level for OECD+ countries (34 OECD plus 8 additional non-OECD economies) and states that all major analyses in tables include all 64 participating countries/economic entities. For some country-level regressions, Norway is excluded due to missing data on the formal mathematics index. For the computer-based mathematics literacy assessment, the paper notes it was optional and taken by students in 31 countries; for the computer-based problem-solving assessment, it was taken by students in 43 countries. Beyond these stated exclusions/subsamples, the excerpt does not specify additional analytic-sample restrictions (e.g., grade bands, school types, or explicit missing-response rules).

data.outcome_summary: This OECD Education Working Paper analyzes how students’ Opportunity to Learn (OTL)—student-reported exposure to (i) formal mathematics topics, (ii) word problems, and (iii) applied mathematics problems—relates to PISA 2012 mathematics literacy. The study uses PISA 2012 mathematics literacy outcomes (including four content subscales: space and shape, quantity, change and relationships, and uncertainty and data) and also examines process subscales (formulate, employ, interpret). Relationships are estimated at multiple levels (country, school, and student) using hierarchical modeling, and the paper reports that OTL indices show significant associations with mathematics literacy in many countries. At the country level, applied mathematics exposure shows a statistically significant quadratic relationship with performance, while formal mathematics is also related to performance (with varying significance by subscale). The paper further links OTL variation to equality of opportunity by showing that within-school variation dominates for OTL indices and that SES relates to performance partly through OTL. The paper emphasizes that PISA is cross-sectional, so the results support associations rather than causal claims.
